claim: LAST is a c-Myc-inducible long noncoding RNA.
source: Here, we report the isolation and characterization of the novel c-Myc-regulated lncRNA LAST (LncRNA-Assisted Stabilization of Transcripts), which acts as a CCND1 mRNA stabilizer.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that LAST is a c-Myc-regulated lncRNA, and this is supported by experimental data showing c-Myc regulation of LAST expression.

claim: LAST acts as a CCND1 mRNA stabilizer.
source: Here, we report the isolation and characterization of the novel c-Myc-regulated lncRNA LAST (LncRNA-Assisted Stabilization of Transcripts), which acts as a CCND1 mRNA stabilizer.
evidence: The abstract and results sections provide experimental data showing that LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.

claim: CCND1 mRNA is not the only target of LAST and CNBP.
source: In addition, data from CNBP RIP-seq and LAST RNA-seq showed that CCND1 mRNA might not be the only target of LAST and CNBP; three additional mRNAs were shown to be post-transcriptional targets of LAST and CNBP.
evidence: The abstract mentions additional targets identified through RIP-seq and RNA-seq experiments.

claim: Three additional mRNAs (SOX9, NFE2L1, and PDF) are post-transcriptional targets of LAST and CNBP.
source: In addition, data from CNBP RIP-seq and LAST RNA-seq showed that CCND1 mRNA might not be the only target of LAST and CNBP; three additional mRNAs were shown to be post-transcriptional targets of LAST and CNBP.
evidence: The results section identifies SOX9, NFE2L1, and PDF as additional targets through sequencing data and validation experiments.

claim: Depletion of LAST diminished tumor formation in a xenograft model.
source: In a xenograft model, depletion of LAST diminished and ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation, which are suggestive of its oncogenic function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by xenograft experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation in a xenograft model.
source: In a xenograft model, depletion of LAST diminished and ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation, which are suggestive of its oncogenic function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by xenograft experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: LAST has an oncogenic function.
source: In a xenograft model, depletion of LAST diminished and ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation, which are suggestive of its oncogenic function.
evidence: The abstract infers oncogenic function based on the tumor formation data from xenograft experiments.

claim: Without LAST, CCND1 exhibits at most partial expression.
source: We thus report a previously unknown lncRNA involved in the fine-tuned regulation of CCND1 mRNA stability, without which CCND1 exhibits, at most, partial expression.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the stabilization data showing reduced CCND1 levels upon LAST depletion.

claim: c-Myc plays a pivotal role in multiple cellular processes including cell cycle progression, malignant transformation, differentiation suppression and apoptosis induction.
source: The oncoprotein c-Myc plays a pivotal role in multiple cellular processes, such as cell cycle progression, malignant transformation, differentiation suppression and apoptosis induction, predominantly through its transcription activity (Seth et al., 1993; Drayton et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2003; Demeterco et al., 2002; Prendergast, 1999; Amati et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1996; Hoffman and Liebermann, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: c-Myc regulates the expression of approximately 10–15% of genes in the genome.
source: Indeed, as a master transcriptional factor, c-Myc regulates the expression of approximately 10–15% of genes in the genome, including a variety of protein-coding genes (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Fernandez et al., 2003), such as CDKN1A, CDKN2B, CCND1, CCND2, CDK4 and E2F2 (Adhikary and Eilers, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CCND1 is a c-Myc target gene of particular importance in cell cycle control.
source: Among c-Myc target genes, CCND1 is of particular importance in cell cycle control and is characterized by the dramatic periodicity of the abundance of its protein product cyclin D1 throughout the cell cycle (Sherr, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cyclin D1 forms a complex with CDK4 or CDK6 and functions as a regulatory subunit required for G1/S transition.
source: Cyclin D1 forms a complex with CDK4 or CDK6 and functions as a regulatory subunit whose activity is required for G1/S transition (Sherr, 1995; Resnitzky et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cyclin D1 interacts with the tumor suppressor pRB1, which in turn positively regulates cyclin D1 expression.
source: Cyclin D1 also interacts with the tumor suppressor pRB1, which in turn positively regulates cyclin D1 expression (DeGregori, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Mutation, amplification and overexpression of CCND1 are frequently observed in cancer and contribute to tumorigenesis.
source: Mutation, amplification and overexpression of CCND1 are frequently observed in cancer and have been reported to contribute to tumorigenesis (Wiestner et al., 2007; Elsheikh et al., 2008; Musgrove et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cyclin D1 is a short-lived protein with a rapid turnover rate of approximately 24 minutes.
source: Cyclin D1 is a short-lived protein with a rapid turnover rate (~24 min) due to degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Diehl et al., 1998; Diehl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: c-Myc can upregulate or downregulate expression of cyclin D1 in a context-dependent manner.
source: c-Myc can upregulate or downregulate expression of cyclin D1 in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent examples and citations.

claim: c-Myc, together with Max, activates CCND1 transcription through an E box located at −558 nt in its promoter.
source: On the one hand, c-Myc, together with Max, a co-transcription factor, activates CCND1 transcription through an E box located at −558 nt in its promoter (Kress et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of c-Myc and ZO-2 enhances repression of the CCND1 promoter through the E box in MDCK cells.
source: On the other hand, simultaneous overexpression of c-Myc and ZO-2 enhances repression of the CCND1 promoter through the E box in MDCK cells (Gonzalez-Mariscal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: c-Myc represses the cyclin DI promoter and antagonizes USF-mediated transactivation in BALB/c-3T3, Rat6 and rat embryo fibroblasts.
source: In addition, c-Myc has been reported to repress the cyclin DI promoter and antagonize USF-mediated transactivation in BALB/c-3T3, Rat6 and rat embryo fibroblasts (Philipp et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple transcription factors, including AP-1, NF-κB, E2F and Oct-1, can bind to their respective CCND1 promoters and regulate its expression.
source: In addition to c-Myc, multiple transcription factors, including AP-1, NF-κB, E2F and Oct-1, can bind to their respective CCND1 promoters and regulate its expression (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: GATA3 cooperates with PARP1 to regulate CCND1 transcription by modulating histone H1 incorporation.
source: CCND1 can also be regulated epigenetically through histone modifications; GATA3 cooperates with PARP1 to regulate CCND1 transcription by modulating histone H1 incorporation (Shan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: MYF5-mediated enhancement in CCND1 mRNA translation contributes to early myogenesis.
source: Moreover, post-transcriptional mechanisms are also involved in the regulation of CCND1, as exemplified by MYF5-mediated enhancement in CCND1 mRNA translation, which contributes to early myogenesis (Panda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Mutations in CCND1 leading to stable truncated transcripts are associated with increased cell proliferation and shortened survival of cancer patients.
source: Mutations in CCND1 leading to stable truncated transcripts are associated with increased cell proliferation and shortened survival of cancer patients (Wiestner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Long noncoding RNAs are defined as transcripts that are longer than 200 nucleotides and lack protein coding capacity.
source: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), which are defined as transcripts that are longer than 200 nucleotides and lack protein coding capacity, are emerging as important regulators of biological processes, including regulation of gene expression at multiple levels, such as chromatin remodeling, transcription, and post-transcriptional modulation (Derrien et al., 2012; Iorio and Croce, 2012; Bonasio and Shiekhattar, 2014; Wilusz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a standard definition stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: c-Myc transcriptionally regulates many lncRNA genes, such as PVT1, the CCAT family, and MYCLos.
source: Genome-wide studies have shown that c-Myc transcriptionally regulates many lncRNA genes, such as PVT1, the CCAT family, and MYCLos, whereas a number of lncRNAs have been demonstrated to be important components of the c-Myc-mediated signaling network (Colombo et al., 2015; Nissan et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015a; Kim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Five significantly c-Myc-downregulated lncRNAs were selected based on fold change above 8 and P-value below 0.01.
source: We selected five significantly c-Myc-downregulated lncRNAs (fold change above 8, P-value below 0.01) that were identified by the lncRNA microarray.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria used in the microarray analysis.

claim: Two lncRNAs, lncRNA-51 and lncRNA-52, were found to be downregulated when c-Myc expression was suppressed by doxycycline treatment.
source: Two of the five lncRNAs, namely, lncRNA-51 and lncRNA-52, along with CDK4 (positive control) were found to be downregulated when c-Myc expression was suppressed by doxycycline treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown of lncRNA-52 showed a significant reduction in colony formation.
source: Of these two c-Myc responsive lncRNAs, lncRNA-52 (RP11-660L16.2, ENST00000529369) was chosen for further investigation because knockdown of this lncRNA (Figure 1B) showed a significant reduction in colony formation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: lncRNA-52 is located approximately 1.8 Mb downstream of the cyclin D1/CCND1 gene in a head-to-tail orientation.
source: lncRNA-52 is located approximately 1.8 Mb downstream of the cyclin D1/CCND1 gene in a head-to-tail orientation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LAST is approximately 700 nt in length.
source: A band of approximately 700 nt in length was detected in both P493-6 and H1299 cells, but was absent in P493-6 cells treated with doxycycline, which suppresses c-Myc expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown by northern blot in Figure 1E.

claim: LAST is predominantly localized in the cytosol.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, LAST was predominantly localized in the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 1F and subcellular fractionation in Figure 1G.

claim: The LAST copy number is higher in tumor cells than in normal cells.
source: The LAST copy number was higher in tumor cells than in normal cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells.
source: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased whereas ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: Ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells.
source: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased whereas ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: The levels of LAST and c-Myc are synchronous during cell cycle progression.
source: Furthermore, the levels of LAST and c-Myc appeared to be notably synchronous during cell cycle progression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: c-Myc binds to chromatin fragments corresponding to the BS2 and BS3 sites in the LAST promoter region.
source: The chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay determined the association of c-Myc with chromatin fragments corresponding to the BS2 and BS3 sites (within F2 fragment) among all examined fragments (Figure 1K, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: BS2 and BS3 sites confer c-Myc-dependent transcriptional activity.
source: Luciferase expression from the reporter containing an individual BS2 or BS3 site was indeed induced by ectopic expression of c-Myc (Figure 1L, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Mutant BS2M and BS3M sites showed no response to c-Myc induction.
source: By contrast, mutant BS2M and BS3M sites showed no response to c-Myc induction (Figure 1L, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: c-Myc transactivates LAST.
source: These data demonstrate that c-Myc transactivates LAST.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChIP and luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: Knockdown of LAST caused a decrease in the percentage of cells in the S and G2/M phases and an increase in the percentage of cells in the G1 phase.
source: Knockdown of LAST caused a decrease in the percentage of cells in the S and G2/M phases and an increase in the percentage of cells in the G1 phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that LAST knockdown prevents cell passage from the G1 phase into S phase.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: LAST promotes G1/S phase transition.
source: As a result, LAST was shown to promote G1/S phase transition.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell cycle analysis data.

claim: Among G1-related cyclins and CDKs genes examined, only the CCND1 mRNA level was significantly decreased upon LAST knockdown.
source: Among all of the mRNAs examined, only the CCND1 mRNA level was significantly decreased (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Among all cyclins or CDKs examined, only cyclin D1 was downregulated when LAST was depleted.
source: Among all of the cyclins or CDKs examined, only cyclin D1 was shown to be downregulated when LAST was depleted (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LAST does not affect c-Myc stability.
source: However, unlike PVT1, we found that LAST, which is also regulated by c-Myc (Figure 1A), does not affect c-Myc stability since knockdown of LAST did not change c-Myc expression at either the mRNA or protein levels (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Depletion of LAST decreased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels in HAFF, H1299 and HCT116 cells.
source: Depletion of LAST decreased whereas over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels in HAFF, H1299 and HCT116 cells.
source: Depletion of LAST decreased whereas over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: LAST does not affect the expression of adjacent genes DHCR7 and NADSYN1.
source: To test if the function of LAST is mediated through an effect on the adjacent genes, we checked the shRNA-mediated LAST knockdown effect on the two adjacent genes DHCR7 and NADSYN1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and found that LAST showed no effect on either the mRNA or protein levels of those two genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions remained unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells.
source: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions were found to remain unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells, whereas the levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA containing 5'UTR, CDS (coding sequences) and 3'UTR regions were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion.
source: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions were found to remain unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells, whereas the levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA containing 5'UTR, CDS (coding sequences) and 3'UTR regions were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: LAST post-transcriptionally regulates CCND1 mRNA.
source: These results suggest that LAST may post-transcriptionally regulate CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that pre-mRNA levels are unchanged while mature mRNA levels are reduced.

claim: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr (Figure 3A), whereas over-expression of LAST increased its half-life from 5 hr to 9 hr (Figure 3B), indicating that LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 9 hr.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr (Figure 3A), whereas over-expression of LAST increased its half-life from 5 hr to 9 hr (Figure 3B), indicating that LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr (Figure 3A), whereas over-expression of LAST increased its half-life from 5 hr to 9 hr (Figure 3B), indicating that LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mRNA half-life experiments.

claim: Endogenous CCND1 mRNA co-precipitated with LAST in a biotinylated oligonucleotide pull-down assay.
source: To determine whether LAST interacts with CCND1 mRNA, we performed a biotinylated oligonucleotide pull-down assay, and as shown in Figure 3C, endogenous CCND1 mRNA but not CCNB1 mRNA co-precipitated with LAST, indicating an association between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CNBP was identified as a protein that mediates the binding between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
source: Proteins pulled down by LAST were separated by SDS PAGE, and a unique band with a molecular weight of approximately 20 kDa was revealed and identified as CNBP by mass spectrometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry identification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CNBP has a preference for binding single-stranded DNA and RNA.
source: CNBP has a preference for binding single-stranded DNA and RNA (Flink and Morkin, 1995) and has been reported to function in the translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA (Sammons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A biotin-labeled antisense DNA probe against LAST pulled down CNBP, but not cyclin D1.
source: To validate the MS Spectro result, we performed a LAST pull-down assay. A biotin-labeled antisense DNA probe against LAST pulled down CNBP, but not cyclin D1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both CNBP and LAST were coprecipitated when CCND1 mRNA was pulled down using a biotinylated antisense DNA probe.
source: To further demonstrate that CNBP can bridge CCND1 mRNA and LAST, we first pulled down CCND1 mRNA using a biotinylated antisense DNA probe as bait; both CNBP and LAST were coprecipitated (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CNBP interacts with both CCND1 mRNA and LAST as shown by RIP assay.
source: The RIP assay further concluded that CNBP interacts with both CCND1 mRNA and LAST (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RIP assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CNBP acts as a mediator for LAST and CCND1 mRNA binding.
source: These data demonstrate that CNBP acts as a mediator for LAST and CCND1 mRNA binding.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pull-down and RIP assay data.

claim: CNBP knockdown in HCT116 led to a decrease in both the mRNA and protein levels of cyclin D1/CCND1.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, CNBP knockdown in HCT116 led to a decrease in both the mRNA and protein levels of cyclin D1/CCND1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA was reduced from 5 hr to 3 hr when CNBP was depleted.
source: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA was reduced from 5 hr to 3 hr as CNBP was depleted (Figure 3G), further demonstrating that CNBP prolongs the CCND1 mRNA half-life.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CNBP prolongs the CCND1 mRNA half-life.
source: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA was reduced from 5 hr to 3 hr as CNBP was depleted (Figure 3G), further demonstrating that CNBP prolongs the CCND1 mRNA half-life.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mRNA half-life experiments.

claim: The association of CCND1 mRNA with LAST via CNBP occurs in the cytosol.
source: Using a LAST and CCND1 mRNA pull-down assay, we found that CNBP was co-precipitated by either LAST or CCND1 mRNA in the cytoplasm, but not the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by subcellular fractionation and pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of CNBP affected the level of mature CCND1 mRNA, but not unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA.
source: Further investigation revealed that knockdown of CNBP affected the level of mature CCND1 mRNA, but not unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA, indicating that the protective role of CNBP in mature CCND1 mRNA stability occurred in the cytosol since nuclear unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA was not affected when CNBP was silenced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increased expression of CCND1 mRNA caused by over-expression of LAST was diminished when CNBP was depleted.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, the increased expression of CCND1 mRNA caused by over-expression of LAST was diminished when CNBP was depleted (lanes 2 vs. 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: LAST affects CCND1 mRNA via CNBP.
source: Thus, our hypothesis is that LAST affects CCND1 mRNA via CNBP.
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by the data showing that LAST's effect on CCND1 requires CNBP.

claim: Knockdown of LAST resulted in no change in CNBP at either the RNA or protein levels.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in no change in CNBP at either the RNA or protein levels (Figure 3H), which suggests that LAST affects CCND1 mRNA not according to the quantity of CNBP, but rather by the association of CNBP and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of CNBP reduced the association between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
source: An RNA pull-down experiment was performed starting with the same amount of CCND1 mRNA, and less LAST was co-precipitated as CNBP was depleted (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Less CNBP was co-precipitated with CCND1 mRNA when LAST was silenced.
source: Similarly, when we pulled down the same amount of CCND1 mRNA, less co-precipitated CNBP was detected as LAST was silenced. As a negative control, the RNA-binding protein HuR remained unchanged after LAST was knocked down (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The 5'UTR but not 3'UTR of CCND1 mRNA binds LAST and CNBP.
source: We found that the 5'UTR but not 3'UTR-1,–2 and −3 of CCND1 mRNA was able to bind LAST and CNBP (Figure 4A and B), indicating that LAST and CNBP bind to the 5' region of CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA pull-down assay data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: LAST and CNBP enhance CCND1 mRNA stability via its 5'UTR.
source: By contrast, the half-life of CCND1 mRNA bearing 5'-UTRs was extended from 4 hr in the absence of LAST and CNBP to 9 hr in the presence of LAST and CNBP, indicating that LAST and CNBP enhanced CCND1 mRNA stability via its 5'UTR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CNBP RIP sequencing showed an enrichment peak at the CCND1 5'UTR.
source: In addition, we performed CNBP RIP sequencing, and an enrichment peak at the CCND1 5'UTR was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LAST, the 5'-UTR of CCND1 mRNA and CNBP form a ternary complex.
source: LAST and CNBP were present in the streptavidin-biotin precipitates (Figure 4C, panel 5 and 6), indicating that these three components indeed form a ternary complex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by sequential immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Two G-rich sequences containing a GGAG core in the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA are responsible for the binding of CNBP.
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) was performed, and the results showed that G-rich-1 and G-rich-2 in the CCND1 5'UTR were responsible for the binding of CNBP (Figure 4D, lower part).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Four G-rich sequences (G-rich-A, C, D and F) from LAST are able to bind CNBP.
source: Among the six predicted G-rich sequences (G-rich-A to F) found in LAST (Figure 4E, upper part), four G-rich sequences (G-rich-A, C, D and F) were found to contain a GGAG core. G-rich-A, C, D and F from LAST were able to bind CNBP, whereas neither G-rich-B nor G-rich-E was able to bind CNBP (Figure 4E, lower part).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CNBP only interacts with G-rich sequences that contain the GGAG core.
source: Thus, CNBP only interacted with G-rich sequences that contained the GGAG core, but not those lacking the GGAG core.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the EMSA data showing selective binding to GGAG-containing sequences.

claim: Over-expression of LAST containing only one site mutation led to an increase in the CCND1 mRNA level.
source: We found that over-expression of LAST containing only one site mutation led to an increase in the CCND1 mRNA level, whereas over-expression of LAST containing four G-rich site mutations nullified its effect on the CCND1 mRNA level (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Over-expression of LAST containing four G-rich site mutations nullified its effect on the CCND1 mRNA level.
source: We found that over-expression of LAST containing only one site mutation led to an increase in the CCND1 mRNA level, whereas over-expression of LAST containing four G-rich site mutations nullified its effect on the CCND1 mRNA level (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: The effect of LAST on CCND1 stability requires at least one of the four functional G-rich motifs.
source: This result indicates that the effect of LAST on CCND1 stability requires at least one of the four functional G-rich motifs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mutation analysis data.

claim: LAST binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 92–134 (domain 3).
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, we concluded that LAST binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 92–134 (domain 3), whereas the CCND1 5'UTR binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 29–134 (domain 2 + domain 3) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by deletion mapping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CCND1 5'UTR binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 29–134 (domain 2 + domain 3).
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, we concluded that LAST binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 92–134 (domain 3), whereas the CCND1 5'UTR binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 29–134 (domain 2 + domain 3) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by deletion mapping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 225 overlapping genes were found between LAST knockdown mRNA-seq and CNBP RIP-seq.
source: The intersection of these two arrays is shown in Figure 5A, and 225 overlapping genes were found (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Three mRNAs (SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF) are likely to be regulated by LAST.
source: Three mRNAs, namely, SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF, were also likely to be regulated by LAST, as knockdown of LAST led to a decrease in their levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of LAST decreased the half-lives of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF mRNAs.
source: Experimental verification showed that knockdown of LAST decreased (Figure 5C) whereas over-expression of LAST increased their half-lives (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased the half-lives of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF mRNAs.
source: Experimental verification showed that knockdown of LAST decreased (Figure 5C) whereas over-expression of LAST increased their half-lives (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CNBP deletion led to a decrease in the mRNA levels of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
source: In addition, CNBP deletion led to a decrease in the mRNA levels of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: LAST, together with CNBP, can regulate the stabilization of additional mRNAs such as SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
source: These data suggest that LAST, together with CNBP, can regulate the stabilization of additional mRNAs, such as SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mRNA stability and expression data for these additional targets.

claim: Knockdown of LAST decreased the tumorigenicity of HCT116 cells in a xenograft mouse model.
source: Knockdown of LAST decreased the tumorigenicity of HCT116 cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by xenograft data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Induction of LAST promoted HCT116 cell tumorigenicity in a xenograft mouse model.
source: By contrast, induction of LAST promoted HCT116 cell tumorigenicity (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by xenograft data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: LAST expression levels are higher in tumor tissues than normal tissues in multiple cancer types.
source: Furthermore, based on the TCGA dataset (Weinstein et al., 2013), we found that the LAST expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than normal tissues, including the human bladder, breast, colorectal, esophagus, head and neck, kidney, liver, lung, prostate and stomach.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figures 6E, 6F, and supplementary figures.

claim: CCND1 expression levels are higher in tumor tissues than normal tissues in multiple cancer types.
source: In addition, the CCND1 expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than in normal tissues, including the human bladder, breast, cervix, bile duct, colorectal, esophagus, head and neck, kidney, pancreas, stomach and uterus.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figures 6E, 6F, and supplementary figures.

claim: Both LAST and CCND1 expression levels are higher in most tumor tissues than in their normal counterparts.
source: In conclusion, both the LAST and CCND1 expression levels were higher in most tumor tissues than in their normal counterparts (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by TCGA data analysis shown in multiple figures.

claim: LAST promotes tumorigenesis.
source: The above results suggest that LAST promotes tumorigenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the xenograft and TCGA expression data.

claim: The absence of LAST downregulated expression of 667 genes.
source: The absence of LAST downregulated expression of 667 genes (log2 (fold change) below - 0.58) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The majority of the top 10 significant pathways affected by LAST knockdown are associated with tumorigenesis.
source: Among these 10 pathways, the majority were associated with tumorigenesis (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Multiple classical transcriptional factors such as c-Myc, E2F1, OCT1, RELA and c-Jun modulate CCND1 at the transcriptional level.
source: Multiple classical transcriptional factors, such as c-Myc, E2F1, OCT1，RELA and c-Jun, have been reported to modulate CCND1 at the transcriptional level (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Pitx2 and HuR control the decay rate of CCND1 mRNA.
source: Moreover, Pitx2 and HuR, which belong to the same ribonucleoprotein complex, also control the decay rate of CCND1 mRNA (Gherzi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: NcRNACCND1 negatively regulates CCND1 transcription by recruiting TLS to the CCND1 promoter.
source: Very recently, NcRNACCND1 was reported to negatively regulate CCND1 transcription by recruiting TLS to the CCND1 promoter (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The G1/S transition is a major checkpoint in cell cycle progression.
source: The G1/S transition is a major checkpoint in cell cycle progression, as it is a 'point of no return' beyond which cells are committed to dividing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: Cyclin D1, along with its catalytically active partner CDK4, is a positive cell cycle regulator that advances the cell cycle from G1 to S phase.
source: Cyclin D1, along with its catalytically active partner CDK4, is a positive cell cycle regulator that advances the cell cycle from G1 to S phase (McKay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Lacking LAST causes cell cycle arrest at the G1/S stage due to decreased cyclin D1.
source: Lacking this lncRNA causes cell cycle arrest at the G1/S stage due to decreased cyclin D1 and attenuates tumor growth.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: CNBP acts on cap-independent translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA.
source: Previous studies have shown that CNBP acts on cap-independent translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA (Sammons et al., 2010) and also functions in sterol-mediated transcriptional regulation as well as c-Myc transcription (Rajavashisth et al., 1989; Murphy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: CNBP functions in sterol-mediated transcriptional regulation and c-Myc transcription.
source: Previous studies have shown that CNBP acts on cap-independent translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA (Sammons et al., 2010) and also functions in sterol-mediated transcriptional regulation as well as c-Myc transcription (Rajavashisth et al., 1989; Murphy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: CNBP is able to guide lncRNA to bind to the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, acting as a mediator between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
source: In this study, we found that CNBP possesses a new function. CNBP is able to guide lncRNA to bind to the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, acting as a mediator between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a novel finding from this study.

claim: lncRNAs are able to regulate their genomic neighborhoods in cis.
source: lncRNAs are able to regulate their genomic neighborhoods in cis (Quinn and Chang, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: CCND1 and LAST are both located on chromosome 11, 1.8 Mb apart and in the same transcriptional direction.
source: Homo sapiens cyclin D1/CCND1 and LAST are both located on chromosome 11, and the two genes are 1.8 Mb apart and in the same transcriptional direction (+strand).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on genomic location data.

claim: CCND1 and LAST are transcribed separately by c-Myc via their respective promoters.
source: It is interesting to note that although CCND1 and LAST are both subjected to positive transcriptional regulation by c-Myc, they do not share the same promoter. Rather, CCND1 and LAST are transcribed separately by c-Myc via their respective promoters (Figures 1K and 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 1K and 6H.

claim: LAST does not regulate CCND1 in cis.
source: Without CNBP, LAST shows no effect on CCND1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), further supporting the concept that LAST does not regulate CCND1 in cis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Co-location of CCND1 and LAST on the same chromosome appears to be a random event.
source: Therefore, co-location of CCND1 and LAST on the same chromosome appears to be a random event.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the trans-acting mechanism.

claim: LAST interacts with CNBP to be guided towards the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, leading to the stabilization of CCND1 mRNA.
source: Normally, LAST interacts with CNBP, a RNA binding protein, by which it is guided towards the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, leading to the stabilization of CCND1 mRNA, which in turn ensures orderly cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the mechanism.

claim: In the case of LAST dysregulation, CCND1 mRNA becomes unstable, resulting in decreased cyclin D1 and cell cycle arrest.
source: In the case of LAST dysregulation, CCND1 mRNA becomes unstable, resulting in decreased cyclin D1, inevitably causing cell cycle arrest and stoppage of cell division (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 6H.

claim: The lack of similarity between human LAST and transcripts of Mus musculus precludes using mouse c-Myc-driven tumor models to further clarify the significance of LAST.
source: The lack of similarity between human LAST and transcripts of Mus musculus also precludes using mouse c-Myc-driven tumor models to further clarify the significance of the LAST in c-Myc-mediated cell cycle regulation and tumor growth in vivo (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by homology analysis shown in Figure 6I.
